title: AudioBench
summary: AudioBench was built for Amplify Dental so a small team could judge speech models on real conditions — and stop redoing transcription, annotation, and benchmarking from scratch.
seoDescription: AudioBench, an ASR evaluation workbench built for Amplify Dental to benchmark speech models on real conditions without redoing transcription and annotation.
highlights: See the best model at a glance, then read where it still fails — without flattening a multi-dimension grid into one notebook.
Label gold audio once in an annotation UI built for speed, then reuse it across prepares, backends, and datasets.
Config-driven and modular: add data, models, prepares, or compute without rebuilding the bench.
writeupMid:
## Built for Amplify Dental

AudioBench is the evaluation and annotation workbench I built for Amplify Dental's transcription work. On a small team, every hour spent re-solving transcription, labelling, or benchmarking is an hour not spent on the product. The design goal is simple: solve each of those once.

Speech quality is not one number. Far speech, room noise, accent, and microphone all change the answer. Opening one model on one clip cannot show that. AudioBench keeps gold audio, prepare pipelines, and backends on one scoreboard so the team compares instead of redoing the work.

The still on the left is that scoreboard: models sorted so the strongest sits at the top, with enough signal to see where it wins and where it does not. A glance is useful. Real data has too many dimensions for a glance. Heatmaps and a full-size grid exist so observations that would hide in a spreadsheet are hard to miss.

## Solve it once, then reuse it

The annotation UI is a product layer I owned, not a spreadsheet next to the audio. Waveform, raw versus clean listen, playback speed, then a saved human transcript. The sample library is the same gold with tags and status, so nobody starts labelling from a blank page. Test Live is hearing a backend on that gold before a grid is spent.

Prepare is a named pipeline, not a one-off file edit. Experiments start from a preset and a dry-run plan. A Whisper Small server on the laptop catches mistakes cheaply; cloud GPUs take the same job when the matrix is large.
writeupAfter:
## How it is built

The stack is modular, scalable, and config-driven. New datasets, models, preprocess steps, or compute instances plug in without rebuilding the bench. Local-first Python and FastAPI; backends behind one manifest; word error rate, character error rate, and real-time factor so accuracy and cost sit on the same row.

### Public data and models

The public set is chosen to stress real conditions, not only studio read speech: AMI (headset and distant meeting mics), VoxPopuli (accented English), Common Voice, VCTK, and LibriSpeech test-clean. Far speech, ambient noise, accents, and microphone variation are in the suite so a good model has to survive them.

The harness in this recording includes Whisper Large v3 (Hugging Face and Faster-Whisper), Whisper Small, Kyutai STT, Google MedASR, Moonshine Base, and Qwen3-ASR. Prepare variants include passthrough, ASR prep, annotation listen, and clean audio, plus composed Lab chains.

Word error rate is how often the transcript is wrong. Character error rate is how far it drifted. Real-time factor is how expensive the model is in time.

### Thanks

Special thanks to David Griswold for generously allowing me to showcase this product.

### About this recording

Listen and annotate shots use public LibriSpeech, not clinic audio. This is the evaluation bench, not Amplify's dental product UI. Whole Nine Yards was stopped with unfinished cells. The cloud clip is two GPU VMs launching beside the local server.

title: Ask Krishna
summary: Hold a question silently and receive five Gita passages in Reflect, or read all 18 chapters in Read Gita — no chatbot or prompt box. The question is never typed, stored, or sent.
seoDescription: Ask Krishna: hold a question silently and receive five Bhagavad Gita passages, or read all 18 chapters. No chatbot; the question is never typed or stored.
highlights: Reflect has no text input: five randomly selected passages appear one at a time.
Read Gita pairs Sanskrit shlokas with English and Hindi meanings, with chapter and shloka navigation.
Marks, resume, and in-browser PNG cards stay on the device; nothing from the interaction needs to be stored outside it.
writeup:
## What it is

Ask Krishna has two complementary modes.

Reflect has no text input. You hold a question in your mind and receive five randomly selected Gita passages, shown one at a time.

Read Gita is the full reading path: all 18 chapters, chapter and shloka navigation, Sanskrit text, and English and Hindi meanings.

## How it is built

The site is static, with no backend. The question never exists as typed data, so it is never stored or sent. App, session, and reading state stay on the device — including marks and resume. Passages and verses can be saved as PNG cards generated in the browser. Interface strings and meanings load from static language files.

## Why it exists

It is a gift-to-self project: a quiet interface for internal reflection that lets the Gita speak without turning the experience into a conversation with software.

title: Aftersight
summary: Aftersight is an image-first search system for photo libraries. It indexes images so they can be found by meaning, visible text, or metadata — not just filenames.
seoDescription: Aftersight, an image-first search system for photo libraries: find images by meaning, visible text or metadata, not just filenames.
highlights: Each image is described once into a structured record that is reused across retrieval.
Dedicated scene, keyword, visible-text, and metadata surfaces are fused with weighted reciprocal rank fusion.
The local interface keeps retrieval inspectable through the source image, generated context, metadata, score, and contributing retrieval surface.
writeup:
## What it is

Each image is described once by a vision-language model into a structured record. Later queries reuse that record across the retrieval system instead of re-describing the image.

## Approach

- Files are fingerprinted and their timestamps reconciled before indexing, giving time-based retrieval a canonical date rather than an unreliable filesystem timestamp.
- MongoDB holds the canonical record, while ChromaDB separates scene, keyword, visible-text, and metadata retrieval surfaces. Ranked results are combined with weighted reciprocal rank fusion (RRF), with search presets shifting emphasis between exact words, meaning, text, and time.
- Search runs locally after the description step. Results retain inspectable provenance through the source image, generated description, metadata, rank, fused score, and contributing retrieval surface.

title: Pixtyle
summary: Pixel Stylizer Toolkit for transforming photos and videos into stylized wallpapers using advanced computer vision techniques.
highlights: Process a photo, folder, or video into stylised stills or clips, with configurable looks built for posterised, wallpaper-like output.
Choose between k-means palette reduction, clustered-and-edged styles, Fourier presets, edge effects, or a combined cartoon pipeline.
Video processing smooths colour clusters across frames and resets on scene changes to reduce palette flicker.
writeup:
## What it is

Pixtyle is a command-line toolkit for stylising photos and videos into wallpaper-like and cartoon-like looks. It supports single images, folders, and video through a shared transform system spanning colour clustering, frequency-domain processing, edge stylisation, and combined pipelines.
writeupMid:
## How the styles work

Each run selects one transform. The names below are the project’s own style names; the paragraphs explain what they do.

### K-means

`kmeans_cluster` reduces the image to a compact colour palette. Pixels are clustered on colour, optionally weighted with spatial position, then replaced with their centroids and optionally blended back toward the original with edge enhancement. The visual aim is posterised, region-like colour rather than line-first stylisation.

### Enhanced

`enhanced_cluster` blends Euclidean and angular distance at reduced resolution, then overlays a Sobel edge tint and colour-pop finishing. It is the stronger segmented-and-outlined alternative when K-means looks too soft on a busy scene.

### Edge Pop

`edge_pop` is a standalone edge styliser. Sobel and Canny can run on GPU through the Torch backend; Scharr, Prewitt, and Laplacian are OpenCV-only. Thresholds and blend modes (`ink`, `glow`) push outline or glow over the pixels you already have.

### Fourier

`fourier_animate` stylises in the frequency domain: FFT band-stop and radial masks with presets (`anime_soft`, `anime_bold`, `cartoon`, `watercolor`, `graphic_novel`), then colour finishing. The look comes from which frequency bands survive, not from palette size.

### Combo

`cartoon_combo` composes optional Fourier-derived detail maps as an auxiliary extractor (not a destructive first pass), K-means colour flattening, Edge Pop lines, then colour-pop or contrast finishing. On video, the edge mask can be EMA-smoothed across frames.

One transform is selected per run. Defaults live in `pixtyle_config.py`; CLI flags override them.

## Video stability

Clustering each video frame independently can make palettes flicker from frame to frame. Pixtyle carries cluster centroids across neighbouring frames (temporal centroid smoothing) so colours stay more stable on a continuous shot. Scene changes are detected by comparing per-channel histograms with an L1 distance and hysteresis (`SceneChangeDetector`, method `hist`). A detected cut calls `reset_state`, so the previous shot’s palette is not blended into the next.
writeupAfter:
## Technical implementation

### Transform architecture

Showcase stylisers subclass `TransformBase` and implement the same interface: `process_numpy`, `process_torch`, `reset_state`, and `describe`. They register in `processors/registry.py`. A run selects one transform; `pixtyle_config.py` holds defaults and CLI flags override them.

That isolation is the point: decode, batch, write, and (for video) temporal hooks stay the same while the styliser is swapped.

### Processing pipeline

**Input** is a single image, a folder, or a video.

OpenCV decodes frames. Image folders are grouped into uniform-shape batches so tensors stay consistent. The selected transform runs on each batch. Video then encodes the stylised clip; when `audio_merge` is enabled, ffmpeg remuxes the original audio onto the processed picture.

Route: input → decode / batch → selected transform → temporal handling where the styliser keeps state → encode → optional audio remux.

### Acceleration and backends

Torch is a hard dependency. Every showcase transform has both NumPy and Torch implementations; the CLI auto-selects a GPU when `detect_torch_device` finds one.

GPU execution applies to the Torch paths for clustering, Fourier processing, and Sobel/Canny edges. Scharr, Prewitt, and Laplacian remain OpenCV-only. GPU is not claimed for the whole toolkit.

### Image-processing primitives

**Colour / clustering.** K-means groups pixels by colour (optionally with spatial weighting) and replaces them with centroids — palette reduction / posterisation. Enhanced clustering uses blended Euclidean and angular distance at reduced resolution, then colour-pop finishing.

**Frequency.** Fourier helpers build a radius grid and apply band-stop / radial masks in FFT space, then colour finishing. Presets (`anime_soft`, `anime_bold`, `cartoon`, `watercolor`, `graphic_novel`) choose which bands survive.

**Edges.** Shared extractors cover Sobel, Canny, and FFT edges (NumPy and Torch). Edge Pop also exposes Scharr, Prewitt, and Laplacian through OpenCV, with `ink` and `glow` blend modes.

**Combined pipeline.** Combo uses optional Fourier-derived detail as a cue, K-means for colour regions, Edge Pop for lines, then colour-pop or contrast finishing (including YUV luminance restore). It does not treat Fourier as a destructive first pass.

### Video-specific state

Temporal centroid smoothing carries cluster centres across neighbouring frames so a continuous shot does not re-seed a new palette every frame.

Combo can EMA-smooth the edge mask across frames (`edge_mask_ema`).

`SceneChangeDetector` compares concatenated per-channel histograms with L1 distance and hysteresis. On a cut, `reset_state` clears centroid history (and Combo’s edge-mask cache) so the next shot starts clean.

### Optional super-resolution

An image-only TensorFlow SavedModel step (`--sr`) can upscale after stylisation. TensorFlow is not required for the main pipeline. The vendored `sr/` training project is a separate environment, not Pixtyle’s core architecture.

title: Flodoro
summary: A local-first Pomodoro workspace that keeps the timer, tasks, history, and your own music on one static page — no account or backend required.
highlights: Work, short-break, and long-break sessions with configurable timing, notifications, task progression, and session history.
Pick a local music folder and play it inside Flodoro with playlist, transport, volume, and scrub controls — no streaming login or bundled music library.
Tasks, history, themes, and preferences stay in the browser, while Chromium can remember selected music folders for later sessions.
writeup:
## What it is

Flodoro is a Pomodoro timer and lightweight task manager that runs as a single static webpage. Work and break settings, tasks, history, themes, and notification preferences stay in the browser, while music is optional and comes from folders the user selects on their own machine.

The goal is a focused workspace without accounts, sync, or a backend.

## Why music belongs here

Timer, current task, and local playback live on the same surface so a focus session does not require switching to a separate music player. Playback remains user-controlled — starting the timer does not start a track — while notification chimes briefly lower the music volume so session alerts are still audible.

## How a session works

Flodoro supports work, short-break, and long-break sessions with configurable durations. A completed work session moves into the next break automatically; after the break, the next work session is started manually. A break can be postponed once, returning to work with five extra minutes.

Tasks can be kept alongside the timer, with completed sessions contributing to the local history and statistics views. Preferences, tasks, and history survive reloads; the live countdown itself does not.

## Local music

Flodoro does not ship a music catalogue or require a streaming login. The user selects a local music folder, and the app builds playlists from that folder and its first-level subfolders.

Playback stays inside the page through the browser audio element, with play/pause, previous/next, mute, volume, and scrubbing controls.

On Chromium browsers, Flodoro can remember the selected folder handle in IndexedDB so it can be reconnected later. The audio files themselves are never copied into browser storage. Other browsers can use the directory file-input fallback for the current session.
writeupAfter:
## Local-first implementation

### Static architecture

Flodoro is built with vanilla HTML, CSS, and JavaScript and runs without an application backend. The hosted page is the same static app.

### Browser storage

Tasks, history, preferences, notification settings, themes, and selected music/track identifiers are stored locally in the browser. Chromium folder handles use IndexedDB so access can be remembered without storing the underlying audio files.

### Music playback

Selected files are played through the browser's `<audio>` element. Folder selection uses the File System Access API where available, with the existing directory-input fallback elsewhere. Music playback remains independent from the Pomodoro timer except for volume ducking during notification chimes.

### Timer behavior

The timer manages work, short-break, and long-break state in the page, with pause, reset, duration adjustments, session transitions, and notifications.

Preferences, tasks, and history persist across reloads; the active countdown does not.

## Design constraint

Flodoro is intentionally serverless. Accounts, cloud sync, and a shipped music catalogue stay out of scope; features are designed to work from the static page and the user's own browser/device.

title: OS Toolkit
summary: An expanding Python filesystem toolkit for developers, data scientists, and scripts or agents: understand storage usage, work with directory trees, and reuse common OS operations without rebuilding them from scratch. Benchmarked against copytree and robocopy.
seoDescription: Python filesystem toolkit for developers, data scientists and agents: storage usage, directory trees and common OS operations, benchmarked against robocopy.
highlights: Usage analysis shows where space goes in a directory tree, including which folders dominate the root.
File transfer handles recursive copies with dry-run, resume without recopying same-size files, and separate optimisations for SSD and HDD destinations.
Supporting utilities recommend folders worth zipping and match two directory trees after profiling them.
writeup:
## What it is

OS Toolkit is an expanding Python filesystem toolkit built around a shared library and a set of small CLIs. It gives developers, data scientists, and scripts or agents reusable ways to inspect and manage local filesystems without rebuilding the same low-level OS logic for every task.

Today it focuses on storage analysis, recursive copy, archive recommendations, and directory comparison. The toolkit is designed to grow as new filesystem and OS-level needs are defined.

## What it helps with

**Understand storage.** Understand where disk space is going. Usage analysis shows directory size and share of the root so large consumers are easy to identify before deciding what to change.

**Transfer trees.** Copy directory trees with dry-run and lightweight resume support, while using separate strategies optimised for SSD and HDD destinations.

**Pack and compare.** Recommend folders that are good candidates for archiving, with archive creation opt-in, and compare two directory trees after profiling them.

## How it works

The toolkit follows a simple pattern: inspect the filesystem, choose the operation, and make potentially expensive changes reviewable before they happen. Storage analysis exposes structure instead of only a total. Copy adapts its behaviour to the destination storage. Zip recommends before creating an archive, while directory comparison works from reusable profiles.

Shared primitives sit underneath the individual CLIs so new tools can reuse existing filesystem logic rather than starting as isolated scripts.

## Real output

A usage scan makes the storage picture concrete:

```text
Analyzing: ./photos

Storage Analysis Results:
`- photos ............... 9.8 KB (100.0%)
    |- large ............ 9.8 KB (100.0%)
    `- small ............  2.0 B (  0.0%)

Analysis completed in 0.00 seconds
```

The tree shows both absolute size and each directory's share of the selected root.
writeupAfter:
## Implementation

Root scripts sit on a shared `os_toolkit` library with written specs. Copy uses separate paths for different destination media: SSD destinations can use threaded copying, while HDD or unknown destinations remain sequential. Resume skips files that already match by size, and dry-run performs no writes. Zip and directory comparison may use process pools; copy does not.

results.title: Copy benchmarks
results.caption: Copy is one part of the toolkit, but it is also the path where implementation choices can be measured directly. I benchmarked it against Python's copytree and Windows robocopy to check whether the disk-aware approach held up in practice. copytree is Python's standard recursive copy; robocopy is the native Windows comparison. The benchmark uses ~1 GB directory trees with balanced, tiny-file-heavy, and media-heavy mixes across SSD and HDD scenarios. Each tool is run repeatedly in isolated subprocesses, outliers are filtered, and the reported values are medians.

tables.title: Copy timings — owner machine
tables.interpretation: Across these owner-machine tests, OS Toolkit led copytree and robocopy on every published workload, with the clearest gains on balanced and tiny-file-heavy SSD copies.
notes: HDD results combine slower HDD-touching paths with faster SSD legs, so they should not be read as a single portable HDD speed.

title: LazyResume
summary: Start with an existing resume PDF, turn it into a structured profile, and regenerate a clean, consistently formatted resume without rebuilding everything by hand.
seoDescription: Turn an existing resume PDF into a structured profile with an LLM pipeline, then regenerate a clean, consistently formatted resume.
highlights: Converts a resume PDF into a canonical structured profile, then into standardized Markdown/PDF output.
Maps inconsistent extracted fields into one stable schema, with review when a mapping is ambiguous.
Separates extraction from generation, so profile data can be corrected or enriched before producing a new resume.
writeup:
## What it is

LazyResume turns an existing resume PDF into a structured profile that can be reviewed, corrected, and regenerated into a consistently formatted resume. By separating the resume’s underlying information from its original layout, the same structured data can be reused to produce clean Markdown and PDF output without rebuilding the resume from scratch.

## From PDF to structured profile

The pipeline extracts text from a resume PDF, then uses an LLM to fill a **canonical JSON schema**—personal details, education, experience, and related fields. Source layout is treated as input to extract from, not as the final data model. Resume content becomes structured data before anything is regenerated.

## Making inconsistent documents usable

Different resumes name and organize the same information differently. The improved ingestion path maps extracted fields onto the canonical schema, including when field names do not match exactly. Clear mappings can be applied automatically; ambiguous or conflicting ones ask for confirmation before they change the profile.

## From structured data back to a resume

The normalized profile is the source for generation. You can correct or enrich that profile before regenerating. Template guidelines produce Markdown from the profile, then Markdown is exported to PDF—so output formatting stays independent of the source PDF’s layout.

## How it is built

Python pipeline with LLM-assisted extraction and generation, PDF text extraction, a canonical JSON/profile representation, local per-user persistence, and template-driven Markdown/PDF generation.

title: Fuzzy Hybrid Model for Stock Trading
summary: A stock-trading research project where I used domain analysis and feature engineering to cut the predictor’s market-input channels by over 70%, then combined deep learning with fuzzy logic for trading decisions.
seoDescription: Stock-trading research: feature engineering cut market-input channels by over 70%, then deep learning was combined with fuzzy logic for trading decisions.
highlights: Reduced the predictor’s market-input channels from 96 to 26 (~73%) through domain-driven feature engineering, leaving each training run with substantially less to process.
Paired a deep sequence model with a fuzzy rule system that converts continuous market signals into buy, sell, or hold actions.
The final system predicted next-day direction correctly about 61% of the time—roughly 13 percentage points above the reported baseline.
writeup:
## What it is

Coursework project with Tristan Till. The system predicts next-day stock direction, then uses a fuzzy trading head to convert market signals into buy, sell, or hold actions for a simulated portfolio.

Primary reported stock: Exxon Mobil (XOM). Market data came from Yahoo Finance, with a chronological train / validation / test split.

## My contribution: feature-space redesign

Early versions fed the sequence model a broad input table: 16 engineered columns across 6 market series, producing **96 backbone input channels**.

Through domain analysis and feature engineering, I redesigned that into a smaller, more targeted representation that shipped in the final system:

- **13** engineered features per ticker, emphasizing relative price and volume changes and multi-scale momentum / trend signals (including RSI and volume-aware RSI across short, medium, and longer windows, plus ROC, MACD, and a volume MACD signal)
- **Target stock + S&P 500 only**
- **26 backbone input channels** total

Exact change: **96 → 26 channels (~72.9% fewer)**. The redesign replaced a broad, weakly focused representation with a smaller set of targeted market and momentum signals.

## Why the redesign mattered

The predictor received far fewer channels at each timestep, reducing input complexity. The final system also used a much smaller recurrent configuration than the early oversized stack. Together, that made training and iteration substantially lighter. No exact runtime multiplier is claimed.

## How the full system worked

At a high level:

**26-channel market representation → GRU-LSTM-Attention predictor → next-day price-change signal → fuzzy trading head → buy / sell / hold**

The predictor reads a 60-day window of the 26 channels and estimates next-day price change.

The trading head is separate. It does not take the full sequence tensor. It receives a compact set of **8 scalars** (momentum and trend-style signals for the target and S&P 500, the predictor’s output, and portfolio liquidity).

Instead of hard thresholds, the fuzzy head maps continuous signals into degrees such as low, medium, and high, then combines them through learned rules. Each of the 8 inputs is scored by three triangular membership functions (**24 membership grades**). Three objective-specific fuzzy heads (return, risk-adjusted return, and drawdown) vote by majority for the final action.

**96 → 26** is the backbone input reduction. **8 → 24 membership grades** is a later fuzzy expansion. They are different stages.

## Results

**Directional hit rate** means how often the predictor got the next-day up/down direction correct.

**Exxon Mobil (final reported system):**

- Reported baselines (zero-change / LSTM): **47.74%**
- Final GRU-LSTM-Attention system: **61.29%**
- Difference: **+13.55 percentage points**

These are final-system results. The redesigned representation is what that system trained on; the repository does not preserve a controlled old-96-channel versus new-26-channel comparison proving the feature redesign alone caused the entire gain.

## Transfer to Chevron

The backbone was fine-tuned for Chevron (CVX) while the fuzzy logic was retained, as a check beyond Exxon. Directional performance there did not beat the LSTM baseline (hybrid **53.55%** vs LSTM **56.13%**). Transfer is supporting context, not the headline.

## What the experiments suggested

Ablations suggested the fuzzy trading head relied meaningfully on engineered market signals rather than simply mirroring day-ahead prediction quality.

## Technical implementation

Python and PyTorch for the sequence model; a custom genetically trained fuzzy inference system (GenFIS) for the trading head; Yahoo Finance market data; chronological train / validation / test split.

## Team attribution

Coursework project with Tristan Till. My contribution focused on the feature-space redesign that became the shipped backbone input representation.

title: Detecting AI Generated Images
summary: A systematic PyTorch training and tuning workflow for distinguishing AI-generated from human images, with repeatable experiment runs that preserve configs, metrics, plots, and checkpoints so each iteration can inform the next.
seoDescription: PyTorch workflow for detecting AI-generated vs human images, with repeatable experiment runs that keep configs, metrics, plots and checkpoints.
highlights: Configuration-driven model training with selectable torchvision backbones and optional FFT/DCT feature heads.
Every experiment is captured as a structured run with its configuration, epoch metrics, curves, confusion matrices, and checkpoints.
The same workflow can run independently across different systems, keeping results consistent and making manual tuning decisions easier to compare.
writeup:
## What it is

This project trains a binary classifier for AI-generated versus human images, and wraps that work in a systematic PyTorch training and tuning workflow. The detection task is the concrete problem; the engineering surface is a repeatable experiment record so each attempt can be understood and followed by another.

## Why it was built

Repeated architecture and configuration experiments are easy to lose if the only leftover is a weight file. This setup keeps the configuration, metrics, plots, and checkpoints with the run so the experiment stays inspectable after training.

## How an experiment works

A run starts from a configuration, trains, and writes a timestamped folder. That folder holds the config snapshot, per-epoch metrics, training curves, confusion matrices, and checkpoints. After inspecting the record, the next change to backbone, features, or training settings is chosen by hand — experiment-driven tuning, not an automated search.

## Model and feature experiments

Training is configuration-driven: torchvision backbones can be swapped, and optional FFT or DCT heads can be added. Dataset preparation and augmentation sit in the same repo, with competition-specific frequency-domain experiments alongside the main trainer.

## Across systems

The same training and tuning workflow can be launched independently on different machines. Each machine writes the same kind of run folder, so results stay readable in one format. There is no central scheduler and no distributed training.
writeupAfter:
## How it is built

`train.py` drives the loop, snapshots `config.json` into `runs/<timestamp>/`, appends epoch lines to `run.txt`, and rewrites curves and confusion matrices as the run proceeds. Best and last checkpoints are stored with the same folder.
